quotes.quote: The first version of LAB includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.
The change-of-control task is one of 1,250 tasks in LAB, spanning 24 legal practice areas.
To date, there has not been a benchmark that illustrates agent progress for long-horizon legal work.
The 24 practice areas in this release are not exhaustive, and many task types within those areas remain uncovered.
Instructions are short, averaging just fifty words.
the rubric contains 57 criteria covering nine legal issues planted across the matter
A deal-team report that identifies eight of ten risks is not 80% useful; it is materially incomplete.
Each task consists of an instruction, a client matter containing relevant materials, and a requirement that the agent produce a work product for review.
LAB is a client matter-centric benchmark.
We're intentionally launching LAB without a leaderboard
Spencer Poff was the technical lead for the open source portion of the Github repo
Julio Pereyra led task design, developing a novel document and scenario generation pipeline that helped us scale task creation.
Instructions are short, averaging just fifty words.
Claude Opus 4.7 leads at 7.1%, with Sonnet 4.6 at 5.4%, Opus 4.6 at 4.2%, GPT-5.5 at 2.1%, and Gemini 3.5 Flash at 0.8% to round out the major model families we've evaluated thus far.
we created a hold-out set of legal tasks that mirror the practice areas and task distribution from the public LAB set
To prevent grader bias, we grade agent runs multiple times across model families and average the results.
Opus 4.7, the highest-performing model by all-pass score, is the most expensive and slowest configuration in the set, at about $50.90 per task and roughly 22 minutes of wall-clock time.
Under our strict all-pass standard, the frontier models we evaluated complete less than 10% of tasks end-to-end in aggregate.
GPT-5.5 leads in the regulated and emerging-company groups, where retrieval-heavy research is a larger part of the work.
Opus 4.7 leads the corporate transactions and funds categories, where synthesis and analytical work dominates.
Sonnet 4.6 leads in the privacy, tax, and private-client work groupings, where structured comparison against statutes and regulations is central.
Agents that close this revise-after-check loop improve all-pass scores by 1.5 points on average.
LAB consists of two parts: a dataset of tasks containing agent instructions, documents, and rubrics as well as an execution harness for running and evaluating agents against those tasks.
Harvey LAB is an open-source project aimed at benchmarking LLM agents' abilities to perform legal work in realistic environments.
In the paper, also name the release (for example v1.3.0) or commit you evaluated. Scores from different releases are not always comparable, and CHANGELOG.md lists each change that moves scores.
Harvey Labs is a filesystem-first benchmark harness.
The system has three phases:
an agent reads a synthetic matter file and writes deliverables.
an LLM judge grades the deliverables against rubric criteria.
the evaluator writes per-run reports and comparison dashboards.
The agent has six closed-workspace tools plus an explicit completion signal:
Execute shell commands inside the run workspace with WORKSPACE_DIR, DOCUMENTS_DIR, and OUTPUT_DIR set

Every agent run executes inside a per-task Podman sandbox (`--network=none --cap-drop=ALL`, writable `/workspace` with read-only `/workspace/documents` and writable `/workspace/output` overlaying it).
the task scores 1.0 only if every criterion passed, else 0.0.
All tasks are evaluated using a rubric-based methodology. Every task defines its rubric inline in `task.json` as a list of equally-weighted pass/fail criteria that an LLM judge grades individually.
There is no partial credit within a criterion either: each one passes or fails.
In legal production settings, a graded mean is misleading.
A diligence memo that catches 95% of issues but misses one material one is not 95% useful — it's wrong.
Every `scores.json` also records three diagnostic fields so you can see how close a model came when it didn't all-pass:
A task is only marked pass if every rubric criterion passes — there is no partial credit at the task level.
The benchmark contains 2,010 tasks across 27 practice areas, with ~114,000 rubric criteria.
The judge runs deterministically to maximize reproducibility across evaluation runs.
There is no golden reference output -- the judge evaluates the agent's work directly against the `match_criteria` description.
Therefore, one task's dual all-pass rate is `0.0`, `0.5`, or `1.0`.
The canonical headline remains the averaged all-pass rate; strict both-agree all-pass is reported separately.

Default judging changed from a single `claude-sonnet-4-6` judge to the standard averaged pair `claude-sonnet-4-6` + `gpt-5.5` (`lab-standard-dual-v1`) for both `evaluation.run_eval` and `utils.sweep`; the primary score artifact is now `scores_dual.json`.
On a ten-task Opus 4.8 trial, pooled criterion pass moved 78.9% -> 80.6% and averaged task all-pass 10.0% -> 15.0%.
Single-judge results before this line are not comparable to dual results after it.
The judge reads every `.docx` file with its tracked changes shown: pandoc marks each insertion and deletion and prints Word comments where they are anchored.
On 2,999 `.docx` outputs sampled from recent runs, 302 (10%) read differently, 296 of them because the file holds tracked insertions or deletions.
A criterion whose deliverables are all missing, or that finds no agent output at all, fails without a judge call.
Per-criterion pass rates drop on those runs.
Tests an agent's ability to complete legal work using documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and file-system tools.
As of November 11, 2026, Gemini 4 Argon ranks first on HLAB-Vals-1.1 with 27.08%, followed by Muse Ember (25.00%) and Muse Spark Open (25.00%).
The Legal Agent Benchmark is a benchmark released by Harvey to test the ability of models to support legal work in an agentic setting. It has a public set and a held-out test set.
The results here are from the held-out set.
Each task asks an agent to produce legal work against a set of task-specific criteria. The agent is provided with six tools:
Harvey grades a task as resolved only if every criterion passes. A model can satisfy most individual criteria and still miss task resolution credit.
The criteria pass rates are much higher: Gemini 4 Argon reaches 96.30%, Wonder Full 96.13%, Wonder 96.01%, and Muse Ember 95.55%.
Harvey fixed the private holdout: 17 unsolvable criteria were removed and one mismatched source document was replaced. Still 120 tasks.
We run Harvey's harness, tools, skills and grading protocol, plus some improvements of our own (see What changed in v1.1).
We use Harvey's generation and grading protocol in the same environment, with internet access disabled.

Harvey grades each submission with two LLM judges. Each judge computes a task pass rate. A task passes only if 100% of its criteria pass, and Harvey's final score is the average of the two judge task pass rates.
The two judges were GPT 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6.
Results are not comparable with the archived v1 board or with Artificial Analysis's independent Harvey LAB-AA.
Context compaction instead of failing on context overflow.
Criteria pass rate now follows Harvey's definition (each judge's pass fraction, averaged) instead of requiring both judges to pass, so it reads higher.
Artificial Analysis' implementation of Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), testing AI agents on real-world legal work from Harvey's dataset of 120 private tasks spanning 24 legal practice areas.
Muse Wonder Full (Max) scores the highest on Harvey LAB-AA v1.1 with a score of 13.1%, followed by Muse Wonder (Max) with a score of 10.0% and Grok 4.7 (Xhigh) with a score of 9.4%
v1.1 supersedes v1.0, and scores are not comparable across versions.
We run Harvey LAB-AA v1.1 with our Stirrup agent harness on Harvey's dataset of 120 private tasks spanning 24 legal practice areas.
A panel of three judges grades each deliverable criterion-by-criterion.
Harvey's studies with legal professionals found hallucinations to be a primary factor in which outputs lawyers prefer, so we collaborated with Harvey to add a hallucination check to scoring.
Judges updated to GPT-6 Sol, Grok 4.7 and Claude Opus 5.5. We found minimal self-preference and average all three to mitigate any bias
Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, which credits a task only when the deliverables satisfy every rubric criterion and contain no material hallucination, averaged across the three judges.
Claude Opus 4.8 delivers the highest score recorded on our Legal Agent Benchmark, and is the first model to break 10% overall on the all-pass standard.
